questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Minimum Possible Value Using the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
questions.problem: Given that $‖v‖=6$ and $u\cdot v=-9$, find the smallest possible value of $‖u‖.$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have   

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |-9| & \le ‖u‖\cdot 6 \\ 9 & \le 6\cdot ‖u‖ \\ 3 & \le 2\cdot ‖u‖.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply both sides of the inequality by $\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3 & \le \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot ‖u‖ \\ \frac{3}{2} & \le ‖u‖\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest possible value of $‖u‖$
is  $\frac{3}{2}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |4| & \le 3\cdot ‖v‖ \\ 4 & \le 3\cdot ‖v‖.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply both sides of the inequality by $\frac{1}{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\cdot 4 & \le \frac{1}{3}\cdot 3\cdot ‖v‖ \\ \frac{4}{3} & \le ‖v‖\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest possible value of $‖v‖$
is  $\frac{4}{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Minimum Possible Value Using the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
questions.problem: Consider the vector $u=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ \sqrt{k} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Given that $u\cdot v=-20$ and $‖v‖=5$,  what is the smallest possible value of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

$$
|u\cdot v|\le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖.
$$

We are given all the quantities in the inequality above, except for $‖u‖.$ So first, we compute $‖u‖$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖u‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(\sqrt{k})^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{14+k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |-20| & \le \sqrt{14+k}\cdot (5) \\ 4 & \le \sqrt{14+k} \\ {4}^{2} & \le {(\sqrt{14+k})}^{2} \\ 16 & \le 14+k \\ 2 & \le k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest possible value of $k$ is $2.$

questions.problem: Consider the vector $u=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ \sqrt{k} \\ -\sqrt{k} \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Given that $u\cdot v=-2$ and $‖v‖=1$, what is the smallest possible value of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

$$
|u\cdot v|\le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖.
$$

We are given all the quantities in the inequality above, except for $‖u‖.$ So first, we compute $‖u‖$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖u‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{k})^{2}+(-\sqrt{k})^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2+2k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |-2| & \le \sqrt{2+2k}\cdot (1) \\ 2 & \le \sqrt{2+2k} \\ {2}^{2} & \le {(\sqrt{2+2k})}^{2} \\ 4 & \le 2+2k \\ 2 & \le 2k \\ k & \ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest possible value of $k$ is $1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Cosine of an Angle
questions.problem: Let $A(1,1,-1,-1)$, $B(2,4,6,8)$, and $C(1,2,3,4).$ Find the cosine of the angle $∠BAC.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $v=\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $w=\overset{\to }{AC}.$ Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =b-a \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 6 \\ 8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =c-a \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Let $\theta =m∠BAC$ be the angle between the vectors $v$ and $w.$ Then, we can find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{v\cdot w}{‖v‖\,‖w‖} \\  & =\frac{{v}_{1}{w}_{1}+{v}_{2}{w}_{2}+{v}_{3}{w}_{3}+{v}_{4}{w}_{4}}{\sqrt{{v}_{1}^{2}+{v}_{2}^{2}+{v}_{3}^{2}+{v}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{w}_{1}^{2}+{w}_{2}^{2}+{w}_{3}^{2}+{w}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+7\cdot 4+9\cdot 5}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{7}^{2}+{9}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{5}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{76}{\sqrt{140}\cdot \sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{76}{2\sqrt{35}\cdot \sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{76}{14\sqrt{30}} \\  & =\frac{38}{7\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $A(-1,3,2,-4)$, $B(1,0,1,-2)$, and $C(0,1,-1,2).$ Find the cosine of the angle $∠BAC.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $v=\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $w=\overset{\to }{AC}.$ Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =b-a \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =c-a \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -3 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Let $\theta =m∠BAC$ be the angle between the vectors $v$ and $w.$ Then, we can find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{v\cdot w}{‖v‖\,‖w‖} \\  & =\frac{{v}_{1}{w}_{1}+{v}_{2}{w}_{2}+{v}_{3}{w}_{3}+{v}_{4}{w}_{4}}{\sqrt{{v}_{1}^{2}+{v}_{2}^{2}+{v}_{3}^{2}+{v}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{w}_{1}^{2}+{w}_{2}^{2}+{w}_{3}^{2}+{w}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot (-3)+2\cdot 6}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{23}{\sqrt{18}\cdot \sqrt{50}} \\  & =\frac{23}{30}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $A(1,0,-1,2)$ and $B(4,8,2,-2).$ Find the cosine of the angle $∠AOB$, where $O(0,0,0,0)$ is the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let

$$
\begin{aligned}a=\overset{\to }{OA}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,b=\overset{\to }{OB}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Also, let $\theta =m∠AOB$ be the angle between the vectors $a$ and $b.$ Then, we can find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{‖a‖\,‖b‖} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{1}{b}_{1}+{a}_{2}{b}_{2}+{a}_{3}{b}_{3}+{a}_{4}{b}_{4}}{\sqrt{{a}_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}+{a}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{b}_{1}^{2}+{b}_{2}^{2}+{b}_{3}^{2}+{b}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 4+0\cdot 8+(-1)\cdot 2+2\cdot (-2)}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{8}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{88}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}\cdot 2\sqrt{22}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{132}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $A(1,-1,2,0)$, $B(1,0,0,-1)$, and $C(0,1,1,0).$ Find the cosine of the angle $∠BAC.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $v=\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $w=\overset{\to }{AC}.$ Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =b-a \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =c-a \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Let $\theta =m∠BAC$ be the angle between the vectors $v$ and $w.$ Then, we can find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{v\cdot w}{‖v‖\,‖w‖} \\  & =\frac{{v}_{1}{w}_{1}+{v}_{2}{w}_{2}+{v}_{3}{w}_{3}+{v}_{4}{w}_{4}}{\sqrt{{v}_{1}^{2}+{v}_{2}^{2}+{v}_{3}^{2}+{v}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{w}_{1}^{2}+{w}_{2}^{2}+{w}_{3}^{2}+{w}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{4}{6} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $A(1,-3,2,-1)$ and $B(1,1,3,-2).$ Find the cosine of the angle $∠AOB$, where $O(0,0,0,0)$ is the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let

$$
\begin{aligned}a=\overset{\to }{OA}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,b=\overset{\to }{OB}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Also, let $\theta =m∠AOB$ be the angle between the vectors $a$ and $b.$ Then, we can find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{‖a‖\,‖b‖} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{1}{b}_{1}+{a}_{2}{b}_{2}+{a}_{3}{b}_{3}+{a}_{4}{b}_{4}}{\sqrt{{a}_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}+{a}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{b}_{1}^{2}+{b}_{2}^{2}+{b}_{3}^{2}+{b}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot 1+2\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot (-2)}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{15}\cdot \sqrt{15}} \\  & =\frac{6}{15} \\  & =\frac{6÷3}{15÷3} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14046175/assets/d1a095e61e6ea64f97a105fd69bc07f3f44990cd6d9794e54e355463c37a2413.png) Given that $\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}=-12$ and $\Vert \mathbf{v}\Vert =4,$ what is the smallest possible value of $k?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

$$
\vert \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

We are given all the quantities in the inequality above, except for $\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert.$ So first, we compute $\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖u‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{k})^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6+k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |-12| & \le \sqrt{6+k}\cdot (4) \\ 12 & \le 4\sqrt{6+k} \\ 3 & \le \sqrt{6+k} \\ {3}^{2} & \le (\sqrt{6+k})^{2} \\ 9 & \le 6+k \\ 3 & \le k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest possible value of $k$ is $3.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the acute angle between the vectors ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14046175/assets/5ed21f4bb536757026315cce838f4cc3028493adac2ff29d46a5b8cbdf11170b.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14046175/assets/8d813e104a708be37ba44b9448806f49ea21a16fe7f613314d2eeab2b59bbda2.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the formula

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{w}}{\Vert\mathbf{v}\Vert \, \Vert \mathbf{w}\Vert},
$$

we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{{v}_{1}{w}_{1}+{v}_{2}{w}_{2}+{v}_{3}{w}_{3}+{v}_{4}{w}_{4}}{\sqrt{{v}_{1}^{2}+{v}_{2}^{2}+{v}_{3}^{2}+{v}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{w}_{1}^{2}+{w}_{2}^{2}+{w}_{3}^{2}+{w}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 2+(-4)\cdot (-2)+(-2)\cdot 2}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{10}{\sqrt{25}\cdot \sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{10}{5\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta=\arccos \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

Also, let $\theta = m\angle{AOB}$ be the angle between the vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}.$ Then, we can find $\cos \theta$ using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{‖a‖\,‖b‖} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{1}{b}_{1}+{a}_{2}{b}_{2}+{a}_{3}{b}_{3}+{a}_{4}{b}_{4}}{\sqrt{{a}_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}+{a}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{b}_{1}^{2}+{b}_{2}^{2}+{b}_{3}^{2}+{b}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot 4+4\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-4)}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-4)^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{-14}{\sqrt{28}\cdot \sqrt{33}} \\  & =\frac{-14}{\sqrt{14}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{33}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{14}}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{33}} \\  & =-\sqrt{\frac{7}{33}}\end{aligned}
